Strictly speaking this is all we need as you can simply add 0 to load, or use `atomic_xchg` to store. However, these have overly strong synchronizing effects which may hurt performance of distributed comms. We may want to consider adding more memory primitives: 1. Scoped memory fences e.g. `tl.fence(scope=”sys”)`. 2. Atomic loads and stores e.g. `tl.atomic_load(ptr, sem=”acquire”, scope=”sys”)` 3. Atomic reduce operations e.g. `tl.reduce_add(ptr, 1, sem=”release”, scope=”sys”)` These would allow more efficient communication patterns by minimizing the synchronization effects of operations. # Typer Official Typer skill to write code with best practices, keeping up to date with new versions and features. ## Installing typer In a virtual environment, `pip install typer` (with pip) or `uv pip install typer` (with uv). For your library/project, add `typer` to the dependencies in `pyproject.toml`. Do not install `typer-slim` or `typer-cli`, they are both deprecated and will now simply install `typer`. Typer supports Python 3.10 and above. ## Use an explicit `Typer` app For maximum generalizability, create an explicit Typer app and register subcommand(s), instead of using `typer.run`: ```python import typer app = typer.Typer() @app.command() def hello(): print(f"Hello World") if __name__ == "__main__": app() ``` instead of: ```python # DO NOT DO THIS: Not extensible. Use Typer() instead. import typer def main(): print(f"Hello World") if __name__ == "__main__": typer.run(main) ``` ## Execute the app To execute the app in the terminal, run ```bash python main.py ``` When multiple commands are registered to the Typer app, you have to add the command name: ```bash python main.py hello ``` To see the automatically generated help documentation, run ```bash python main.py --help ``` or set `no_args_is_help` to `True` when creating the `Typer()` add to automatically show the help when

have to add the command name: ```bash python main.py hello ``` To see the automatically generated help documentation, run ```bash python main.py --help ``` or set `no_args_is_help` to `True` when creating the `Typer()` add to automatically show the help when running a command without any arguments. ## Use `Annotated` Always prefer the `Annotated` style for declarations of CLI arguments and options. It allows us to pass additional metadata that can be used by Typer. ```python from typing import Annotated import typer app = typer.Typer() @app.command() def hello(name: Annotated[str, typer.Argument()] = "World"): # Note that name is an optional Argument, as a default is provided print(f"Hello {name}") if __name__ == "__main__": app() ``` This program can be run as-is, or can provide a specific name: ```bash python main.py python main.py Rick ``` An older way of setting a default value is this: ```python # DO NOT DO THIS: old style. Use Annotated instead. @app.command() def main(name: str = typer.Argument(default="World")): # Note that name is an optional Argument, as a default is provided print(f"Hello {name}") ``` Similarly, the old style could use ellipsis (...) to explicitly mark an argument as required. ```python # DO NOT DO THIS: old style. Use Annotated without

declare them in the `typer.Option`: ```python from typing import Annotated import typer app = typer.Typer() @app.command() def main(user_name: Annotated[str, typer.Option("--name", "-n")]): # On the CLI, the required user name can be specified with -n or --name print(f"Hello {user_name}") if __name__ == "__main__": app() ``` You can run this program as such: ```bash python main.py -n "Rick" python main.py --name "Morty" ``` ### CLI options with multiple values By declaring a CLI option as a list, it can receive multiple values: ```python from typing import Annotated import typer app = typer.Typer() @app.command() def main(user: Annotated[list[str] | None, typer.Option()] = None): if not user: print(f"No users provided!") raise typer.Abort() for u in user: print(f"Processing user: {u}") if __name__ == "__main__": app() ``` This can be executed like so: ```bash python main.py --user Rick --user Morty --user Summer ``` ## Rich By default, Rich can be used with its custom markup syntax to set colors and styles, e.g. ```python from rich import print print("[bold red]Alert![/bold red] [green]Portal gun[/green] shooting! :boom:") ``` Typer supports using Rich formatting in the docstrings and the help messages of CLI arguments and CLI options. ```python from typing import Annotated import typer app = typer.Typer(rich_markup_mode="rich") @app.command() def create( username:

""" print(f"Creating user: {username}") @app.command(help="[bold red]Delete[/bold red] a user with [italic]username[/italic].") def delete( username: Annotated[ str, typer.Argument(help="The username to be [red]deleted[/red]") ], ): """ Some internal utility function to delete. It is a sovereign, on-premise AI workbench that lets an organization deploy agentic, tool-using, multimodal AI over confidential internal data without that data ever leaving the organization's infrastructure. It sees documents, drawings, and spreadsheets; plans multi-step investigations; uses tools inside a controlled sandbox; verifies its own outputs against evidence; and leaves an auditable record of every action it takes. The system is judged not on whether it can answer a question, but on whether it can be trusted to act — and trust is engineered in, not assumed: every action passes through policy gating and independent verification before it is reported as done. Every document, entity, and AI-generated artifact is stored as a markdown note inside an on-premise vault, using an Obsidian-style linked-notes model. The vault is the knowledge system — vector search and the knowledge graph both sit on top of the same files rather than being a separate, disconnected index. /veliky-vault/ Equipment/ Pump-P204.md <- [[Compressor-C104]], [[SOP-Pump-Maintenance]] Compressor-C104.md SOPs/ SOP-Pump-Maintenance.md Reports/ Inspection-Report-62.md Maintenance-Report-184.md People/ Employee-Rakesh.md <- solved -> [[Ticket-4471]] Manager-Sharma.md <- oversees -> [[Employee-Rakesh]] Agent-Generated/ P204-Vibration-Analysis-2026-09-03.md 6.1 Why the vault model, specifically The knowledge graph comes for free — [[wikilinks]] and backlinks ARE the entity graph; no separate graph database to build and keep in sync. Differentiators — the “No One Else Thought of This” Layer These seven ideas are what separate VELIKY from every other “local RAG chatbot” submission. They are ranked by build cost against demo impact; Section 14 states which are committed for the demo versus roadmap-only. 7.0 Tacit knowledge capture — the strongest single differentiator When an employee closes a hard ticket, the agent auto-drafts a short “how this was actually solved” note and asks for a one-click confirm/edit — not a form, just approve-or-tweak. Over months this builds an institutional-memory graph of how this specific plant's engineers actually solve problems, not generic SOP text. This is the one idea that isn't “AI reads documents better” — it's “this organization stops losing what its best people know when they retire or leave.” That is a boardroom-level pain point, not a tech-demo one, and it's the line the pitch should be built around. 7.1 Self-extending tools

New code is inherently high-risk, so this always requires human approval before the tool is registered. Once approved, it is available to every future run. This reuses the sandbox, policy engine, and tool registry that already exist; the only new piece is the propose-and-register loop. 7.2 Autonomous shift handover Industrial plants run continuous shifts, and handover is traditionally a person manually writing notes for the next one — information routinely gets lost. The agent generates the handover briefing itself, pulled directly from the audit log and the ticket/equipment graph: what happened, what's unresolved, what's flagged, what to focus on next. Future similar cases retrieve this correction as evidence, weighted above generic documents. This is not on-prem fine-tuning — that's too heavy for the timeline — it's a growing case-memory of human corrections inside the same retrieval pipeline, which directly answers “how does this improve over time” without claiming model training that isn't there. 7.4 Proactive, sensor-triggered investigation Everything else waits for a person to ask. This layer lets the agent notice an anomaly first. A synthetic sensor stream (Section 7.4.1) feeds a deterministic threshold/rate-of-change watcher — not the LLM — and a trip auto-generates an internal goal (“Investigate P-204 vibration anomaly”) that runs through the exact same orchestrator, evidence-gathering, and verification pipeline as a typed question. watcher — not the LLM — and a trip auto-generates an internal goal (“Investigate P-204 vibration anomaly”) that runs through the exact same orchestrator, evidence-gathering, and verification pipeline as a typed question. The novel claim is not the alerting (threshold monitoring is old, well-understood technology) — it's that the alarm launches a full evidence-backed investigation instead of just a red light. 7.4.1 How the sensor layer is actually built (no live plant access required) A simulator process publishes realistic readings (baseline + noise, with one equipment's line given a slow deliberate drift on a timer) into a small sensor_readings table or pub/sub channel. It is a sovereign, on-premise AI workbench that lets an organization deploy agentic, tool-using, multimodal AI over confidential internal data without that data ever leaving the organization's infrastructure. Every document, entity, and AI-generated artifact is stored as a markdown note inside an on-premise vault, using an Obsidian-style linked-notes model. The vault is the knowledge system — vector search and the knowledge graph both sit on top of the same files rather than being a separate, disconnected index. /veliky-vault/ Equipment/ Pump-P204.md <- [[Compressor-C104]], [[SOP-Pump-Maintenance]] Compressor-C104.md SOPs/ SOP-Pump-Maintenance.md Reports/ Inspection-Report-62.md Maintenance-Report-184.md People/ Employee-Rakesh.md <- solved -> [[Ticket-4471]] Manager-Sharma.md <- oversees -> [[Employee-Rakesh]] Agent-Generated/ P204-Vibration-Analysis-2026-09-03.md 6.1 Why the vault model, specifically The knowledge graph comes for free — [[wikilinks]] and backlinks ARE the entity graph; no separate graph database to build and keep in sync. Differentiators — the “No One Else Thought of This” Layer These seven ideas are what separate VELIKY from every other “local RAG chatbot” submission. They are ranked by build cost against demo impact; Section 14 states which are committed for the demo versus roadmap-only. 7.0 Tacit knowledge capture — the strongest single differentiator When an employee closes a hard ticket, the agent auto-drafts a short “how this was actually solved” note and asks for a one-click confirm/edit — not a form, just approve-or-tweak. Over months this builds an institutional-memory graph of how this specific plant's engineers actually solve problems, not generic SOP text. This is the one idea that isn't “AI reads documents better” — it's “this organization stops losing what its best people know when they retire or leave.” That is a boardroom-level pain point, not a tech-demo one, and it's the line the pitch should be built around. 7.1 Self-extending

New code is inherently high-risk, so this always requires human approval before the tool is registered. Once approved, it is available to every future run. This reuses the sandbox, policy engine, and tool registry that already exist; the only new piece is the propose-and-register loop. 7.2 Autonomous shift handover Industrial plants run continuous shifts, and handover is traditionally a person manually writing notes for the next one — information routinely gets lost. The agent generates the handover briefing itself, pulled directly from the audit log and the ticket/equipment graph: what happened, what's unresolved, what's flagged, what to focus on next. This is nearly free given the audit trail that already exists, and it's a pain point anyone with industrial operations experience will

Future similar cases retrieve this correction as evidence, weighted above generic documents. This is not on-prem fine-tuning — that's too heavy for the timeline — it's a growing case-memory of human corrections inside the same retrieval pipeline, which directly answers “how does this improve over time” without claiming model training that isn't there. 7.4 Proactive, sensor-triggered investigation Everything else waits for a person to ask. This layer lets the agent notice an anomaly first. A synthetic sensor stream (Section 7.4.1) feeds a deterministic threshold/rate-of-change watcher — not the LLM — and a trip auto-generates an internal goal (“Investigate P-204 vibration anomaly”) that runs through the exact same orchestrator, evidence-gathering, and verification pipeline as a typed question. Evaluation Methodology An architecture is not a research or engineering contribution until there's a way to show it could be wrong. This section exists because it was the single biggest gap between a strong architecture and a complete one — borrowed and adapted from EDITH's own evaluation design (Section 15), which already specifies this rigorously for the personal-agent version of the same pattern. 8.1 What is being tested Does policy-gated execution, hybrid vault/graph memory, and mandatory verification measurably improve multi-step industrial investigation tasks, relative to the same underlying model used as a plain conversational assistant? 8.2 Systems compared System A (baseline) — the underlying open-weight model called directly, given the same documents as raw context, no vault, no policy engine, no verification step. System B (VELIKY) — the same model behind the full orchestrator, vault/graph memory, policy engine, tool use, and verification loop. Holding the model constant across both systems is the control that isolates the

vault, no policy engine, no verification step. System B (VELIKY) — the same model behind the full orchestrator, vault/graph memory, policy engine, tool use, and verification loop. Holding the model constant across both systems is the control that isolates the architecture's contribution from raw model quality — skipping this is the most common mistake in an informal comparison. 8.3 Benchmark design A fixed set of 15–20 tasks drawn from the demo domain (pump/equipment investigation, evidence lookup, calculation-backed conclusions), graded into three tiers: single-step lookup, multi-step with no dependencies, multi-step with explicit dependencies. Each task has a predefined, checkable success criterion written before any run — e.g. “correctly cites the SOP threshold, correctly recomputes the percentage change, and does not omit the conflicting reading in Report B” — not a subjective judgment made after seeing the output. 8.4 Metrics Metric Definition Task success rate Pass/fail against the pre-written success criterion. False-success rate System reports success but manual inspection shows the goal wasn't actually met — this is the metric that most directly proves the verification engine is doing real work. Steps/tool calls to completion Count of planner-tool-execution cycles used. Human interventions required Times a person had to correct, approve outside the

wasn't actually met — this is the metric that most directly proves the verification engine is doing real work. Steps/tool calls to completion Count of planner-tool-execution cycles used. Human interventions required Times a person had to correct, approve outside the expected flow, or restart. Wall-clock time to completion End-to-end latency from goal submission to final verified result. 8.5 Procedure and honesty about scale Each task is run 3–5 times per system to account for LLM stochasticity, reported as a mean and range rather than a single point estimate. This should be presented as a small-sample comparative study — conclusions scoped to “observed difference on this task set,” not generalized claims of statistical significance. Two cheap secondary comparisons reuse the same run logs: verification on vs. off (does it reduce false-success rate), and replanning vs. static plan (deliberately withhold a required file mid-task and compare recovery). 9. .. -*- rest -*- ================================================== API changes in the new masked array implementation ================================================== Masked arrays are subclasses of ndarray --------------------------------------- Contrary to the original implementation, masked arrays are now regular ndarrays:: >>> x = masked_array([1,2,3],mask=[0,0,1]) >>> print isinstance(x, numpy.ndarray) True ``_data`` returns a view of the masked array -------------------------------------------- Masked arrays are composed of a ``_data`` part and a ``_mask``. Accessing the ``_data`` part will return a regular ndarray or any of its subclass, depending on the initial data:: >>> x = masked_array(numpy.matrix([[1,2],[3,4]]),mask=[[0,0],[0,1]]) >>> print x._data [[1 2] [3 4]] >>> print type(x._data) <class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> In practice, ``_data`` is implemented as a property, not as an attribute. Therefore, you cannot access it directly, and some simple tests such as the following one will fail:: >>>x._data is x._data False ``filled(x)`` can return a subclass of ndarray ---------------------------------------------- The function ``filled(a)`` returns an array of the same type as ``a._data``:: >>> x = masked_array(numpy.matrix([[1,2],[3,4]]),mask=[[0,0],[0,1]]) >>> y = filled(x) >>> print type(y) <class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> >>> print y matrix([[ 1, 2], [ 3, 999999]]) ``put``, ``putmask`` behave like their ndarray counterparts ----------------------------------------------------------- Previously, ``putmask`` was used like this:: mask = [False,True,True] x = array([1,4,7],mask=mask) putmask(x,mask,[3]) which translated to:: x[~mask] = [3] (Note that

<class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> >>> print y matrix([[ 1, 2], [ 3, 999999]]) ``put``, ``putmask`` behave like their ndarray counterparts ----------------------------------------------------------- Previously, ``putmask`` was used like this:: mask = [False,True,True] x = array([1,4,7],mask=mask) putmask(x,mask,[3]) which translated to:: x[~mask] = [3] (Note that a ``True``-value in a mask suppresses a value.) In other words, the mask had the same length as ``x``, whereas ``values`` had ``sum(~mask)`` elements. Now, the behaviour is similar to that of ``ndarray.putmask``, where the mask and the values are both the same length as ``x``, i.e. :: putmask(x,mask,[3,0,0]) ``fill_value`` is a property ---------------------------- ``fill_value`` is no longer a method, but a property:: >>> print x.fill_value 999999 ``cumsum`` and ``cumprod`` ignore missing values ------------------------------------------------ Missing values are assumed to be the identity element, i.e. 0 for ``cumsum`` and 1 for ``cumprod``:: >>> x = N.ma.array([1,2,3,4],mask=[False,True,False,False]) >>> print x [1 -- 3 4] >>> print x.cumsum() [1 -- 4 8] >> print x.cumprod() [1 -- 3 12] ``bool(x)`` raises a ValueError ------------------------------- Masked arrays now behave like regular ``ndarrays``, in that they cannot be converted to booleans: :: >>> x = N.ma.array([1,2,3]) >>> bool(x) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> ValueError: The truth value of an

Use a.any() or a.all() ================================== New features (non exhaustive list) ================================== ``mr_`` ------- ``mr_`` mimics the behavior of ``r_`` for masked arrays:: >>> np.ma.mr_[3,4,5] masked_array(data = [3 4 5], mask = False, fill_value=999999) ``anom`` -------- The ``anom`` method returns the deviations from the average (anomalies).

Steps to validate transcendental functions: 1) Add a file 'umath-validation-set-<ufuncname>.txt', where ufuncname is name of the function in NumPy you want to validate 2) The file should contain 4 columns: dtype,input,expected output,ulperror a. dtype: one of np.float16, np.float32, np.float64 b. input: floating point input to ufunc in hex. Example: 0x414570a4 represents 12.340000152587890625 c. expected output: floating point output for the corresponding input in hex. This should be computed using a high(er) precision library and then rounded to same format as the input. d. ulperror: expected maximum ulp error of the function. This should be same across all rows of the same dtype. Otherwise, the function is tested for the maximum ulp error among all entries of that dtype. 3) Add file umath-validation-set-<ufuncname>.txt to the test file test_umath_accuracy.py which will then validate your ufunc.

HISTORY OF THE SOFTWARE ========================== Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see http://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python's principal author, although it includes many contributions from others. In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see http://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software. In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations (now Zope Corporation, see http://www.zope.com). In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see http://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation is a sponsoring member of the PSF. All Python releases are Open Source (see http://www.opensource.org for the Open Source Definition). Guido remains Python's principal author, although it includes many contributions from others. In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see http://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software. In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations (now Zope Corporation, see http://www.zope.com). In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see http://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. .. -*- rest -*- ================================================== API changes in the new masked array implementation ================================================== Masked arrays are subclasses of ndarray --------------------------------------- Contrary to the original implementation, masked arrays are now regular ndarrays:: >>> x = masked_array([1,2,3],mask=[0,0,1]) >>> print isinstance(x, numpy.ndarray) True ``_data`` returns a view of the masked array -------------------------------------------- Masked arrays are composed of a ``_data`` part and a ``_mask``. Accessing the ``_data`` part will return a regular ndarray or any of its subclass, depending on the initial data:: >>> x = masked_array(numpy.matrix([[1,2],[3,4]]),mask=[[0,0],[0,1]]) >>> print x._data [[1 2] [3 4]] >>> print type(x._data) <class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> In practice, ``_data`` is implemented as a property, not as an attribute. Therefore, you cannot access it directly, and some simple tests such as the following one will fail:: >>>x._data is x._data False ``filled(x)`` can return a subclass of ndarray ---------------------------------------------- The function ``filled(a)`` returns an array of the same type as ``a._data``:: >>> x = masked_array(numpy.matrix([[1,2],[3,4]]),mask=[[0,0],[0,1]]) >>> y = filled(x) >>> print type(y) <class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> >>> print y matrix([[ 1, 2], [ 3, 999999]]) ``put``, ``putmask`` behave like their ndarray counterparts ----------------------------------------------------------- Previously, ``putmask`` was used like this:: mask = [False,True,True] x = array([1,4,7],mask=mask) putmask(x,mask,[3]) which translated to:: x[~mask] = [3] (Note that

<class 'numpy.matrixlib.defmatrix.matrix'> >>> print y matrix([[ 1, 2], [ 3, 999999]]) ``put``, ``putmask`` behave like their ndarray counterparts ----------------------------------------------------------- Previously, ``putmask`` was used like this:: mask = [False,True,True] x = array([1,4,7],mask=mask) putmask(x,mask,[3]) which translated to:: x[~mask] = [3] (Note that a ``True``-value in a mask suppresses a value.) In other words, the mask had the same length as ``x``, whereas ``values`` had ``sum(~mask)`` elements. Now, the behaviour is similar to that of ``ndarray.putmask``, where the mask and the values are both the same length as ``x``, i.e. :: putmask(x,mask,[3,0,0]) ``fill_value`` is a property ---------------------------- ``fill_value`` is no longer a method, but a property:: >>> print x.fill_value 999999 ``cumsum`` and ``cumprod`` ignore missing values ------------------------------------------------ Missing values are assumed to be the identity element, i.e. 0 for ``cumsum`` and 1 for ``cumprod``:: >>> x = N.ma.array([1,2,3,4],mask=[False,True,False,False]) >>> print x [1 -- 3 4] >>> print x.cumsum() [1 -- 4 8] >> print x.cumprod() [1 -- 3 12] ``bool(x)`` raises a ValueError ------------------------------- Masked arrays now behave like regular ``ndarrays``, in that they cannot be converted to booleans: :: >>> x = N.ma.array([1,2,3]) >>> bool(x) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> ValueError: The truth value of an

------------------------------- Masked arrays now behave like regular ``ndarrays``, in that they cannot be converted to booleans: :: >>> x = N.ma.array([1,2,3]) >>> bool(x) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all() ================================== New features (non exhaustive list) ================================== ``mr_`` ------- ``mr_`` mimics the behavior of ``r_`` for masked arrays:: >>> np.ma.mr_[3,4,5] masked_array(data = [3 4 5], mask = False, fill_value=999999) ``anom`` -------- The ``anom`` method returns the deviations from the average (anomalies).

Steps to validate transcendental functions: 1) Add a file 'umath-validation-set-<ufuncname>.txt', where ufuncname is name of the function in NumPy you want to validate 2) The file should contain 4 columns: dtype,input,expected output,ulperror a. dtype: one of np.float16, np.float32, np.float64 b. input: floating point input to ufunc in hex. Example: 0x414570a4 represents 12.340000152587890625 c. expected output: floating point output for the corresponding input in hex. This should be computed using a high(er) precision library and then rounded to same format as the input. d. ulperror: expected maximum ulp error of the function. This should be same across all rows of the same dtype. Otherwise, the function is tested for the maximum ulp error among all entries of that dtype. 3) Add file umath-validation-set-<ufuncname>.txt to the test file test_umath_accuracy.py which will then validate your ufunc.

HISTORY OF THE SOFTWARE ========================== Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see http://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python's principal author, although it includes many contributions from others. In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see http://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software. In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations (now Zope Corporation, see http://www.zope.com). In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see http://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation is a sponsoring member of the PSF. All Python releases are Open Source (see http://www.opensource.org for the Open Source Definition). HISTORY OF THE SOFTWARE ========================== Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see http://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python's principal author, although it includes many contributions from others. In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see http://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software. In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations (now Zope Corporation, see http://www.zope.com). In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see http://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation is a sponsoring member of the PSF. All Python releases are Open Source (see http://www.opensource.org for the Open Source Definition).
